title: How Igloos Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss igloos: their history as Inuit snow houses (described as hunting shelters rather than permanent homes), the Inuit people and the terms Eskimo versus Inuit, Inuit culture and kayak angst, Eskimo kisses, how igloos stay warm through insulation and body heat, and a step-by-step overview of building one (block cutting, dome construction, keystone, chimney plug, entryway, air holes). The episode closes with a listener mail about a company donating LifeStraw water purifiers after the LifeStraw episode.
topics: ventilation and air holes in igloos
ice hotels and ski resort igloos

segments.title: Opening banter and sickness
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Chuck being under the weather after recording the fainting goats episode, then set up the topic of igloos as an early technology tied to clothing and shelter.

segments.title: Inuit name for igloos and Inuit people
segments.summary: The hosts explain that igloo is an Inuit word meaning snow house, and describe the Inuit as a widely spread Indigenous group living from Siberia to Alaska, Canada and Greenland. They discuss why Eskimo is considered derogatory and why Inuit is preferred, with the disputed origin of the Eskimo term.

segments.title: Inuit society and kayak angst
segments.summary: The hosts describe Inuit family and social structure, with no formal government and families at the center, and food sharing through hunting. They discuss seal hunting and kayak angst, a condition described as specific to Inuit men who fear returning to kayaking after being lost at sea.

segments.title: Eskimo kisses and Inuit population
segments.summary: The hosts describe the traditional Inuit nose-rubbing greeting, where people pressed their nose and inhaled near a loved one's face, and note the popular version is inaccurate. They mention Inuit population today, citing a Canadian heritage figure of about 68,400, and that igloos were hunting shelters rather than permanent homes.

segments.title: Igloo villages and Chili Willy tangent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss igloos that were linked into compounds or larger igloo cities used for gatherings, then briefly talk about the cartoon Chili Willy and whether its igloo was accurate.

segments.title: Why igloos stay warm
segments.summary: The hosts explain that igloos can be up to forty degrees warmer than outside, due to body heat, reduced wind chill, and snow acting as an insulator. Partial melting during the day and refreezing at night, along with body heat, strengthens the structure.

segments.title: Building an igloo step by step
segments.summary: The hosts cover igloo construction: a snow saw and shovel, hard-packed wet snow cut into blocks (about three feet long, fifteen inches high, eight inches deep per a wilderness guide), a circular foundation with blocks shaped on a slant and decreasing in size, sticks for temporary support, a keystone block plugging the top chimney, smoothing loose snow into the cracks, cutting the door afterward, and an L-shaped entryway. Ski resort igloos and Alex Schreiber's Ohio igloo are also mentioned.

segments.title: Air holes and safety
segments.summary: The hosts warn that igloos need air holes for ventilation, since sealed structures can cause suffocation, especially if a camp stove or Coleman lantern is used inside. They suggest the reader consult the How Stuff Works article for illustrated instructions.

segments.title: LifeStraw listener mail
segments.summary: A listener named Stephen, from Eleventh Hour Search in Alexandria, Virginia, wrote that his company would donate at least six thousand LifeStraw water purifiers after the LifeStraw episode. The hosts express appreciation and invite listeners to send in stories of saving the world for a T-shirt.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the igloo episode, recommend the How Stuff Works igloo guide, and close the show.
